# Setting up a C and C++ development environment {#sec-ch-cpp-env} > *"Debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first place."* — > Brian Kernighan and P. J. Plauger [@kernighan1978]. ::: {.callout-note} ## Learning objectives By the end of this chapter you will be able to: - describe the **toolchain** that turns C and C++ source code into a running program — preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker, loader — and the file each stage produces; - install a compiler and a debugger on **Linux** and on **Windows** (GCC via MSYS2, or Microsoft's MSVC), and configure **Visual Studio Code** to build, run and debug C and C++ programs; - compile from the command line with the right **flags** (language standard, warnings, optimisation, debug information, sanitizers) and read compiler **diagnostics**; - split a program into **header** and **source** files and build it with **Make** or **CMake**; - **prove** which files must be recompiled after a change, and why Make's timestamp rule gets it right. ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Topics covered Preparing a workstation to write, compile, run and debug C and C++ programs with Visual Studio Code, on Windows and on Linux. ::: ## Intuition: a translator, not a reader In Part I, Python read your program and carried it out line by line, a bit like a cook who reads a recipe aloud while cooking (@sec-python-language). C and C++ work differently: before anything runs, a **translator** rewrites the whole recipe into the cook's native language — the machine code of your processor (@sec-von-neumann) — and binds it into a booklet, the **executable**. Running the program means handing the booklet to the cook. This has three consequences you will feel from day one: 1. there is a **build step** between editing and running: forget it and you run yesterday's program; 2. many mistakes are caught **before** the program runs, by the translator — and the error messages refer to a moment ("compile time") different from the one in which the program misbehaves ("run time"); 3. the executable is tied to a **platform** (processor + operating system): the booklet written for one cook is unreadable to another. Chapter [-@sec-ch-compiled] studies these trade-offs in depth. This chapter is practical: we set up the tools, follow a program through the translator, and learn to drive a debugger. ## The toolchain: from source to process {#sec-toolchain} A **toolchain** is the chain of programs that turns source files into a running process. For C and C++ the stages are always the same, whatever the compiler brand [@bryant2016, ch. 1 and 7; @levine1999]: ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| fig-cap: "The C/C++ toolchain. The compiler driver (`gcc`, `g++`, `clang++`, `cl`) runs the first four stages for you; the loader is part of the operating system." flowchart LR A["hello.cpp
source"] -->|preprocessor| B["hello.ii
pure C++"] B -->|compiler| C["hello.s
assembly"] C -->|assembler| D["hello.o
object file"] D -->|linker| E["hello
executable"] L["libstdc++, libc
libraries"] -->|linker| E E -->|loader| F["process
in memory"] ``` | Stage | Input → output | What it does | |---|---|---| | **preprocessor** | `.c`/`.cpp` → translation unit | executes the `#` directives: pastes the text of `#include`d headers, expands `#define` macros, keeps or drops `#if` blocks | | **compiler proper** | translation unit → assembly (`.s`) | parses, type-checks, optimises, and emits instructions for the target processor | | **assembler** | `.s` → object file (`.o`, `.obj`) | encodes the instructions in binary; leaves **symbols** (names of functions and variables defined elsewhere) unresolved | | **linker** | object files + libraries → executable | resolves every symbol to an address and lays out the final file (ELF on Linux, PE on Windows, Mach-O on macOS) | | **loader** | executable → process | the operating system maps the file into memory, loads shared libraries, and jumps to the entry point, which eventually calls `main` | : The stages of the toolchain {#tbl-toolchain} The command `g++ hello.cpp -o hello` runs the first four stages in one go: `g++` is a **driver** that calls the real tools for you. Options let us stop after any stage, so we can look at each intermediate product. Here is the program we will follow: ```{.cpp filename="hello.cpp"} // hello.cpp — the classic first program, plus one function of our own #include // preprocessor: paste the declarations of the I/O library int square(int x) { // a function we define in this translation unit return x * x; } int main() { // execution starts here std::cout << "Hello, C++! 7 squared is " << square(7) << '\n'; return 0; // 0 = success, reported to the operating system } ``` ### Stage 1: the preprocessor `g++ -E` stops after preprocessing. The single line `#include ` is replaced by the full text of the header and of every header it includes in turn: ```{.bash} $ g++ -std=c++20 -E hello.cpp -o hello.ii && wc -l hello.cpp hello.ii ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 11 hello.cpp 43177 hello.ii 43188 total ``` ::: Our 11-line file has become a translation unit of tens of thousands of lines — and **every** source file that includes `` pays that price again. This is why large C++ projects compile slowly, and why C++20 introduced **modules** (`import std;` in C++23), which are compiled once and reused [@stroustrup2022, §3.2.2]. ### Stage 2: the compiler proper `g++ -S` stops after compilation and leaves human-readable **assembly**. Let us look at the instructions generated for `square`, with optimisations on (`-O2`): ```{.bash} $ g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -S hello.cpp -o hello.s && sed -n '/^_Z6squarei:/,/ret/p' hello.s | grep -v '^\s*\.cfi' ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` _Z6squarei: .LFB2431: endbr64 imull %edi, %edi movl %edi, %eax ret ``` ::: Apart from a label and `endbr64` (a marker used by the processor's control-flow protection), the function is three instructions, written in the AT&T syntax *operation source, destination*: multiply the argument by itself (`edi` is the register in which the x86-64 calling convention passes the first integer argument), copy the result into `eax` (the register that holds the return value), return. The odd name `_Z6squarei` is the **mangled** name of `square(int)`: C++ encodes the parameter types in the symbol name so that overloaded functions (@sec-ch-c-vs-cpp) get distinct symbols. ### Stage 3: the assembler and the symbol table `g++ -c` produces an **object file**. `nm` lists its **symbols**: `T` marks a function defined here (in the *text* section), `U` a symbol that is **used but undefined** — the linker will have to find it elsewhere. ```{.bash} $ g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -c hello.cpp -o hello.o && nm -C hello.o | grep -E ' (T|U) ' ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0000000000000000 T square(int) U std::ostream::put(char) U std::ostream::operator<<(int) U std::basic_ostream >& std::__ostream_insert >(std::basic_ostream >&, char const*, long) U std::ios_base_library_init() U std::cout U std::basic_ostream >& std::operator<< >(std::basic_ostream >&, char const*) U __stack_chk_fail 0000000000000000 T main ``` ::: `square` and `main` are defined here; the stream `std::cout`, the output operators and the support routines come from the C++ standard library (`libstdc++` for GCC). ### Stage 4: the linker Linking connects the `U`s to their definitions and produces the executable: ```{.bash} $ g++ hello.o -o hello && ./hello && echo "exit status: $?" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hello, C++! 7 squared is 49 exit status: 0 ``` ::: `$?` is the shell's variable holding the **exit status** of the last command: the `return 0` of `main` reached the operating system. We will use exit statuses to make C++ and Python programs cooperate in @sec-ch-cpp-python. ::: {#exm-link-error} ## A link error is not a compile error If a function is **declared** (its signature is known) but never **defined** (its body is missing), every translation unit compiles, and the error appears only at link time: ```{.cpp} #include int cube(int x); // declaration only: "trust me, it exists" int main() { std::cout << cube(3) << '\n'; } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ld: : in function `main': nodef.cpp:(.text.startup+0x1e): undefined reference to `cube(int)' collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status ``` ::: The linker, not the compiler, complains: `undefined reference to cube(int)`. Learning to tell **which tool** produced an error message is the first step to fixing it. ::: ## Compilers, standards and versions {#sec-compilers} ### The three major compilers - **GCC**, the GNU Compiler Collection, started by Richard Stallman in 1987; the default compiler on Linux. Drivers: `gcc` for C, `g++` for C++ [@gccmanual]. - **Clang**, the C/C++ front end of the **LLVM** project, started by Chris Lattner at the University of Illinois [@lattner2004]; the default on macOS and widely used on Linux and Windows. Drivers: `clang`, `clang++`. - **MSVC**, Microsoft's C/C++ compiler, shipped with Visual Studio; driver `cl.exe`, Windows only. All three implement the same **ISO standards**, with small differences in extensions, diagnostics and the date at which they support new features. At the time of writing (November 2026) the latest major releases are GCC 16.1 (April 2026), which made C++20 the default C++ dialect, and LLVM/Clang 23.1 (August 2026) [@gcc16; @llvm23]. ### The language standards C and C++ are defined by international standards maintained by two ISO working groups: WG14 (C) and WG21 (C++). A program written against a standard works with any conforming compiler — this is the basis of the portability we discuss in @sec-ch-compiled. | Language | Standard | Informal name | Highlights | |---|---|---|---| | C | ANSI X3.159-1989 / ISO 9899:1990 | C89/C90 | the language of K&R 2nd edition [@kernighan1988] | | C | ISO/IEC 9899:1999 | C99 | `//` comments, ``, ``, declarations anywhere | | C | ISO/IEC 9899:2011 / 2018 | C11 / C17 | threads, atomics, `_Static_assert`; C17 is a bug-fix release | | C | ISO/IEC 9899:2024 | C23 | `bool`, `true`, `false` and `nullptr` as keywords, `constexpr` objects [@iso9899c23] | | C++ | ISO/IEC 14882:1998 / 2003 | C++98/03 | the first standard: templates, the STL, exceptions | | C++ | ISO/IEC 14882:2011 | C++11 | move semantics, `auto`, lambdas, smart pointers: "modern C++" | | C++ | 2014, 2017 | C++14, C++17 | refinements; `std::optional`, `std::string_view`, structured bindings | | C++ | ISO/IEC 14882:2020 | C++20 | concepts, ranges, modules, coroutines, `<=>` | | C++ | ISO/IEC 14882:2024 | C++23 | `import std;`, `std::print`, `std::expected` [@iso14882] | : The C and C++ standards {#tbl-standards} C++26 completed its technical work in March 2026, but in October 2026 its international approval ballot did not pass, mainly over the new *contracts* feature; at the time of writing the committee is deciding how to proceed [@sutter2026]. Nothing in this part depends on C++26. ::: {.callout-important} ## The toolchain used in this book Every C++ example in this part is compiled with **GCC (`g++`) using `-std=c++20 -O2 -Wall -Wextra`** and every C example with **`gcc -std=c17`**, on x86-64 Linux, and actually executed when the book is built: the outputs you see are real. Where a result depends on the platform (sizes of types, timings), the text says so. ::: ```{.bash} $ g++ --version | head -1 && gcc --version | head -1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 gcc (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 ``` ::: ## Installing the tools {#sec-installing} ### On Linux Linux distributions package GCC, the GNU debugger GDB, Make and CMake. On Debian and Ubuntu: ```bash sudo apt update sudo apt install build-essential gdb cmake # gcc, g++, make, libc headers, gdb, cmake g++ --version # check ``` (On Fedora: `sudo dnf install gcc-c++ gdb make cmake`.) Clang is one command away (`sudo apt install clang`), and having two compilers is useful: a program that compiles cleanly with both is more likely to be standard-conforming. ### On Windows Windows does not ship a C++ compiler. Three good options: 1. **GCC through MSYS2** (the route of the VS Code documentation [@vscodecpp]). Install MSYS2 from its web site, open the *MSYS2 UCRT64* terminal and install the toolchain with `pacman -S --needed base-devel mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-toolchain`; then add `C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin` to the Windows `PATH` environment variable, open a **new** terminal and check `g++ --version` and `gdb --version`. You get the same compiler used in this book, producing native Windows executables (`.exe`). 2. **MSVC**, by installing *Visual Studio* or the lighter *Build Tools for Visual Studio* with the "Desktop development with C++" workload. Compile from the *Developer Command Prompt* with `cl /std:c++20 /EHsc /W4 hello.cpp`. 3. **WSL** (Windows Subsystem for Linux): a real Linux distribution inside Windows; then follow the Linux instructions. VS Code connects to it transparently. ::: {.callout-warning} ## The most common installation problem `'g++' is not recognized as an internal or external command`: the compiler is installed but its folder is not in `PATH`, or the terminal was opened **before** `PATH` was changed. Close every terminal (and VS Code), reopen, and run `where g++` (Windows) or `which g++` (Linux) to see which compiler, if any, is found. ::: ### Visual Studio Code VS Code is an **editor**, not a compiler: it calls the compiler you installed. Install VS Code and, from the Extensions view, Microsoft's **C/C++** extension (`ms-vscode.cpptools`), which adds code completion (IntelliSense), build tasks and debugging. When you first run *Run C/C++ File* on an open source file, VS Code asks which compiler to use and writes its configuration in a `.vscode` folder of your project: | File | Purpose | |---|---| | `tasks.json` | how to **build**: the compiler command and its arguments | | `launch.json` | how to **run and debug**: which executable, which debugger (`gdb`, `lldb` or the MSVC debugger) | | `c_cpp_properties.json` | how IntelliSense should **understand** the code: compiler path, standard, include folders | : The VS Code configuration files {#tbl-vscode-files} The default build task compiles the *active file* only, with debug information and no warnings. It is worth editing `tasks.json` once to use the flags of the next section. A version that works on Linux and, with `g++.exe`, on Windows: ```json { "version": "2.0.0", "tasks": [ { "type": "cppbuild", "label": "C/C++: g++ build active file", "command": "g++", "args": [ "-std=c++20", "-Wall", "-Wextra", "-Wpedantic", "-g", "-O0", "${file}", "-o", "${fileDirname}/${fileBasenameNoExtension}" ], "problemMatcher": ["$gcc"], "group": { "kind": "build", "isDefault": true } } ] } ``` The `problemMatcher` turns the compiler's diagnostics into clickable entries in the *Problems* panel. For projects with several files, prefer a build system (@sec-build-systems): VS Code's *CMake Tools* extension drives CMake directly. ## Compiler flags that matter {#sec-flags} A compiler has hundreds of options; a handful matter every day. | Flag (GCC/Clang) | MSVC | Effect | |---|---|---| | `-std=c++20`, `-std=c17` | `/std:c++20` | which **language standard** to accept | | `-Wall -Wextra` | `/W4` | enable the most useful **warnings** | | `-Wpedantic` | `/permissive-` | reject non-standard extensions | | `-Werror` | `/WX` | treat warnings as errors | | `-O0`, `-O2`, `-O3` | `/Od`, `/O2` | **optimisation** level: none (best for debugging) to aggressive | | `-g` | `/Zi` | include **debug information** (source lines, variable names) | | `-fsanitize=address,undefined` | `/fsanitize=address` | add run-time checks for memory errors and undefined behaviour | | `-o name` | `/Fe:name` | name of the output file | : Everyday compiler flags {#tbl-flags} ### Warnings are free bug reports A **warning** is the compiler saying: "this is legal, but it is very probably not what you meant." Here are three classic mistakes that compile — and that `-Wall -Wextra` points out: ```{.cpp} #include int main() { int n; // (1) never initialised unsigned limit = 10; for (int i = 0; i < limit; ++i) { // (2) signed/unsigned comparison if (i = 5) // (3) assignment, not comparison! std::cout << "five\n"; } std::cout << n << '\n'; } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` warnings.cpp: In function ‘int main()’: warnings.cpp:6:23: warning: comparison of integer expressions of different signedness: ‘int’ and ‘unsigned int’ [-Wsign-compare] 6 | for (int i = 0; i < limit; ++i) { // (2) signed/unsigned comparison | ~~^~~~~~~ warnings.cpp:7:15: warning: suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value [-Wparentheses] 7 | if (i = 5) // (3) assignment, not comparison! | ~~^~~ warnings.cpp:10:23: warning: ‘n’ is used uninitialized [-Wuninitialized] 10 | std::cout << n << '\n'; | ^~~~ warnings.cpp:4:9: note: ‘n’ was declared here 4 | int n; // (1) never initialised | ^ ``` ::: Mistake (3) would make the loop print `five` forever, since `i = 5` sets `i` and evaluates to 5, which is true; mistake (1) prints an unpredictable value. **Compile with warnings on, and treat every warning as an error until you can explain why it is harmless.** ### Sanitizers: run-time checks for free Some errors cannot be detected at compile time. The **sanitizers** of GCC and Clang instrument the program with checks: AddressSanitizer detects out-of-bounds accesses, use of freed memory and leaks, with a typical slowdown of about 2× [@serebryany2012]; UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer detects, for example, signed integer overflow. Without the sanitizer this program silently writes past the end of an array; with it, it stops at the faulty line: ```{.cpp} #include int main() { int a[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4}; int sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i <= 4; ++i) // off by one: a[4] does not exist sum += a[i]; std::cout << sum << '\n'; } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ==PID==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow on address 0x7f97da900030 at pc 0x5564895a8445 bp 0x7ffed11a7c40 sp 0x7ffed11a7c30 READ of size 4 at 0x7f97da900030 thread T0 #0 0x5564895a8444 in main oob.cpp:7 Address 0x7f97da900030 is located in stack of thread T0 at offset 48 in frame #0 0x5564895a8278 in main oob.cpp:3 SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow oob.cpp:7 in main [process exited with status 1] ``` ::: (We show only the key lines of the report; the full report also maps the memory around the bad address.) Read it from the top: the kind of error (`stack-buffer-overflow`), the access (`READ of size 4`), and the first frame of the stack trace, `in main oob.cpp:7` — file and line. Sanitizers are available on Linux and macOS with GCC and Clang; MSVC supports AddressSanitizer with `/fsanitize=address`. We will use them throughout this part, in particular for the memory errors of @sec-ch-c-intro and @sec-ch-c-vs-cpp. ## Debugging {#sec-debugging} A **debugger** runs your program under control: it can stop it at a **breakpoint**, execute it **one line at a time**, and show the values of variables and the **call stack** (the chain of function calls that led to the current line, @sec-recursion). In VS Code you click in the margin to set a breakpoint and press F5; underneath, VS Code talks to GDB (or LLDB, or the MSVC debugger). We can drive GDB directly to see what happens. Compile with `-g -O0` (debug information, no optimisation, so that the machine code follows the source line by line): ```{.cpp filename="debugme.cpp"} #include int square(int x) { int r = x * x; return r; } int main() { int total = 0; for (int i = 1; i <= 3; ++i) total += square(i); std::cout << total << '\n'; } ``` ```{.bash} $ g++ -std=c++20 -g -O0 debugme.cpp -o debugme && gdb -batch -q -ex 'break square' -ex run -ex backtrace -ex 'info args' -ex finish -ex 'print total' ./debugme ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Breakpoint 1 at 0x1174: file debugme.cpp, line 4. Breakpoint 1, square (x=1) at debugme.cpp:4 4 int r = x * x; #0 square (x=1) at debugme.cpp:4 #1 0x00005555555551a8 in main () at debugme.cpp:11 x = 1 0x00005555555551a8 in main () at debugme.cpp:11 11 total += square(i); Value returned is $1 = 1 $2 = 0 ``` ::: | What you want | GDB command | VS Code | |---|---|---| | stop at a line or function | `break square`, `break debugme.cpp:11` | click in the margin | | start / continue | `run` / `continue` | F5 | | next line (over calls) | `next` | F10 | | enter the called function | `step` | F11 | | run to the end of this function | `finish` | Shift+F11 | | show the call stack | `backtrace` | *Call Stack* panel | | show a variable | `print total`, `info locals` | *Variables* / *Watch* panels | : Debugger commands and their VS Code equivalents {#tbl-gdb} Note the last line of the session: after `finish`, `total` is still `0`. Execution stopped in the middle of line 11, *after* `square(1)` returned (`Value returned is $1 = 1`) but *before* the addition — the debugger shows the state of the machine at an exact instant, which is what makes it so precise. ::: {.callout-tip} ## A debugging method A debugger is not a substitute for thinking. Kernighan and Pike's advice [@kernighan1999, ch. 5] still holds: **reproduce** the failure with the smallest input, **form a hypothesis** about the cause, **test** it (with a breakpoint, a `print`, an assertion), and only then change the code. ::: ## Programs in several files {#sec-multifile} Real programs are split into files, for the same reasons as Python modules (@sec-modularity): each file has one responsibility, can be understood alone, and — specific to compiled languages — can be **compiled separately**. ### Declarations and definitions C and C++ distinguish two things that Python merges: - a **declaration** introduces a name and its type: `int square(int x);` ("a function `square` exists, taking an `int` and returning an `int`"); - a **definition** also provides the body (or, for a variable, the storage). A name must be **declared before it is used** in each translation unit, and **defined exactly once** in the whole program — the **one-definition rule** (ODR) [@iso14882, §basic.def.odr]. The convention that follows is: - a **header file** (`.h`, `.hpp`) contains declarations — the **interface**; - a **source file** (`.c`, `.cpp`) contains the definitions — the **implementation**; - every file that needs the interface `#include`s the header. ```{.cpp filename="geometry.hpp"} // geometry.hpp — interface: what other files may use #pragma once // include this header at most once per translation unit double circle_area(double radius); double rectangle_area(double width, double height); ``` ```{.cpp filename="geometry.cpp"} // geometry.cpp — implementation #include "geometry.hpp" // quotes: search the project folder first constexpr double pi = 3.141592653589793; double circle_area(double radius) { return pi * radius * radius; } double rectangle_area(double width, double height) { return width * height; } ``` ```{.cpp filename="main.cpp"} // main.cpp — the program #include // angle brackets: a system header #include "geometry.hpp" int main() { std::cout << "circle r=1: " << circle_area(1.0) << '\n' << "rectangle 2x3: " << rectangle_area(2.0, 3.0) << '\n'; } ``` Each source file is compiled **separately** into an object file, then the objects are linked: ```{.bash} $ g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -c geometry.cpp && g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -c main.cpp && g++ geometry.o main.o -o shapes && ./shapes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` circle r=1: 3.14159 rectangle 2x3: 6 ``` ::: `#pragma once` (supported by all major compilers, though not part of the standard) prevents a header from being pasted twice into the same translation unit, which would repeat its definitions of types. The portable equivalent is an **include guard**: ```cpp #ifndef GEOMETRY_HPP #define GEOMETRY_HPP // ... declarations ... #endif ``` ### Build systems: Make and CMake {#sec-build-systems} Typing the commands above by hand does not scale, and recompiling *every* file after each change wastes time. A **build system** records how each file is produced from others and redoes only the necessary work. The classic one is **Make**, written by Stuart Feldman at Bell Labs in 1976 [@feldman1979]. A `Makefile` lists **rules**: a *target*, its *prerequisites*, and the commands that rebuild the target from them. ```{.makefile filename="Makefile"} # Makefile — each rule: target: prerequisites, then commands indented with a TAB CXX = g++ CXXFLAGS = -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2 shapes: main.o geometry.o $(CXX) main.o geometry.o -o shapes main.o: main.cpp geometry.hpp $(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -c main.cpp geometry.o: geometry.cpp geometry.hpp $(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -c geometry.cpp clean: rm -f shapes *.o ``` Make rebuilds a target when it is **missing** or **older** than one of its prerequisites. Watch it at work: a full build, then nothing to do, then a change to `main.cpp` only: ```{.bash} $ rm -f *.o shapes && make && echo '--- second run:' && make && echo '--- after touching main.cpp:' && touch main.cpp && make ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2 -c main.cpp g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2 -c geometry.cpp g++ main.o geometry.o -o shapes --- second run: make: 'shapes' is up to date. --- after touching main.cpp: g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2 -c main.cpp g++ main.o geometry.o -o shapes ``` ::: After `main.cpp` changed, only `main.o` and the executable were rebuilt; `geometry.o` was reused. Why is that exactly the right set? The **dependency graph** answers. ::: {#def-build-graph} ## Build graph A **build graph** is a finite directed acyclic graph whose vertices are files and with an edge $u \to v$ when $v$ is built from $u$ ($u$ is a prerequisite of $v$). Vertices without incoming edges are **sources** (written by hand); the others are **targets**, each produced by a deterministic command from its direct prerequisites. ::: ::: {#prp-rebuild-set} ## What must be rebuilt If the set $C$ of source files changes, a target must be rebuilt if and only if it is **reachable** from some file of $C$ (there is a directed path from a changed file to it). Moreover, rebuilding the reachable targets in a topological order (@thm-toposort) brings every target up to date with one command each. ::: *In one line:* a change propagates exactly along the arrows — what is downstream of an edited file is stale, everything else can be reused. ::: {.deep kind="proof"} ## Proof of @prp-rebuild-set *Not reachable ⇒ unaffected.* By induction along a topological order: if no prerequisite of a target $t$ is a changed file or a stale target, then $t$'s command receives exactly the same inputs as last time and, being deterministic, produces the same output — so the old $t$ is still correct. A target not reachable from $C$ has, by definition, no changed or reachable prerequisite, so the induction applies to it. *Reachable ⇒ must be rebuilt.* If $t$ is reachable, some path $c \to v_1 \to \dots \to v_k = t$ starts at a changed file $c$. In general the new content of $c$ can change $v_1$, which can change $v_2$, and so on; a build system that does not inspect the *meaning* of the files cannot exclude it, so it must rebuild $t$. (A smarter system may still discover that a rebuilt file is byte-identical to the old one and stop the propagation there.) *Order.* Processing reachable targets in a topological order guarantees that when $t$ is rebuilt, all its prerequisites are already up to date; hence each target is built once. $\blacksquare$ ::: ::: {.deep} ## Why Make's timestamp rule implements @prp-rebuild-set Make does not know which files you changed; it compares **modification times**. To bring target $t$ up to date it first, recursively, brings every prerequisite up to date, and then rebuilds $t$ if $t$ is missing or some prerequisite is newer than $t$. Suppose that after the previous complete build every target was newer than its prerequisites, and that editing a file sets its time to "now", later than every existing file. Then, by induction along a topological order, a target gets a time later than its old one exactly when one of its prerequisites does — i.e. exactly when it is reachable from an edited file. The assumptions matter: copying an *old* file over a source (which keeps the old timestamp), a clock that goes backwards, or a prerequisite missing from the Makefile (a header not listed!) all break the guarantee. This is why compilers can **generate** the header dependencies for you (`g++ -MMD`), and why modern tools such as Ninja and Bazel also compare file contents. ::: Writing Makefiles by hand is error-prone and not portable to MSVC. Most C++ projects use **CMake**, which *generates* the build files for the platform (Makefiles, Ninja files, Visual Studio solutions) from a short description: ```{.cmake filename="CMakeLists.txt"} # CMakeLists.txt cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20) project(shapes LANGUAGES CXX) set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20) set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON) add_executable(shapes main.cpp geometry.cpp) target_compile_options(shapes PRIVATE $<$:/W4> $<$>:-Wall -Wextra>) ``` ```{.bash} $ cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja > /dev/null && cmake --build build && ./build/shapes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1/3] Building CXX object CMakeFiles/shapes.dir/geometry.cpp.o [2/3] Building CXX object CMakeFiles/shapes.dir/main.cpp.o [3/3] Linking CXX executable shapes circle r=1: 3.14159 rectangle 2x3: 6 ``` ::: The two commands are the same on every platform: `cmake -S . -B build` (configure: generate the build files in a separate `build` folder) and `cmake --build build` (build). CMake works out the header dependencies by itself. We will use this setup for the project (@sec-ch-project-crm). ## Reading compiler errors {#sec-reading-errors} C++ error messages have a reputation for being long. Three rules make them manageable: 1. **Fix the first error first.** Later errors are often consequences of the first (a missing `;` can confuse the parser for many lines). 2. **Find `file:line:column`.** Every diagnostic starts with a location; the text after `error:` is the message, and `note:` lines add context. 3. **Identify the tool.** A message mentioning `undefined reference` comes from the linker (@exm-link-error); everything else from the compiler. ```{.cpp} #include #include int main() { std::string name = "Ada"; int length = name.size() // missing semicolon std::cout << nmae << '\n'; // misspelt name } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` errors.cpp: In function ‘int main()’: errors.cpp:7:5: error: expected ‘,’ or ‘;’ before ‘std’ 7 | std::cout << nmae << '\n'; // misspelt name | ^~~ errors.cpp:6:9: warning: unused variable ‘length’ [-Wunused-variable] 6 | int length = name.size() // missing semicolon | ^~~~~~ ``` ::: GCC reports the missing semicolon — at the place where it noticed it, the beginning of the *next* line, since only there does the statement become impossible — and says nothing about the misspelt name: after the first error it skipped the rest of that statement. Add the semicolon and compile again; now the second mistake surfaces, with a suggestion: ```{.cpp} #include #include int main() { std::string name = "Ada"; auto length = name.size(); std::cout << nmae << ' ' << length << '\n'; } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` errors2.cpp: In function ‘int main()’: errors2.cpp:7:18: error: ‘nmae’ was not declared in this scope; did you mean ‘name’? 7 | std::cout << nmae << ' ' << length << '\n'; | ^~~~ | name ``` ::: This is rule 1 in action: one real mistake can hide or cause others, so fix the first one and recompile. ::: {.project-link} **In the project.** The CRM of @sec-ch-project-crm is a multi-file C++ program: one header and one source file per component, a small `main.cpp`, and a `CMakeLists.txt` (requirement R12, @sec-crm-brief). It is built with the flags of @tbl-flags — warnings on, and sanitizers during development — and its README gives the two CMake commands of @sec-build-systems, which work unchanged on Linux and on Windows. ::: ## Common pitfalls ::: {.callout-warning} ## Watch out - **Running a stale executable.** You edited the source but did not rebuild: in a compiled language, *save* is not *build*. - **Compiler not in `PATH`** after installation; reopen the terminal and VS Code. - **Ignoring warnings.** Most beginners' bugs (uninitialised variables, `=` instead of `==`, signed/unsigned comparisons) are reported as warnings. - **Debugging optimised code.** With `-O2` the debugger may skip lines or show variables as ``: debug with `-O0 -g`. - **Definitions in headers.** A function *defined* (not just declared) in a header included by two source files breaks the one-definition rule: `multiple definition of …` at link time (unless it is `inline`). - **Headers missing from the Makefile** dependencies: Make does not rebuild what it does not know about. Use CMake, or `-MMD`. ::: ## Summary - The **toolchain** turns sources into a process in stages: preprocessor → compiler → assembler → linker → loader. `-E`, `-S`, `-c` stop after each stage; `nm` shows the symbols an object file defines and needs. - **GCC**, **Clang** and **MSVC** implement the ISO **C** and **C++** standards; this book uses `g++ -std=c++20` and `gcc -std=c17`. - On Linux install `build-essential` and `gdb`; on Windows use MSYS2's GCC, MSVC, or WSL. VS Code stores build, debug and IntelliSense settings in `tasks.json`, `launch.json` and `c_cpp_properties.json`. - Always compile with **warnings** (`-Wall -Wextra`) and, while developing, with **sanitizers**; debug with `-g -O0`. - **Headers** hold declarations, **sources** definitions (one-definition rule). A build system rebuilds exactly the targets **reachable** from the changed files (@prp-rebuild-set); **CMake** generates the build files for any platform. ## Exercises ::: {#exr-cpp1-stages} For each message, say which stage of the toolchain produced it and why: (a) `fatal error: geometri.hpp: No such file or directory`; (b) `error: 'cout' is not a member of 'std'`; (c) `undefined reference to 'circle_area(double)'`; (d) `multiple definition of 'pi'`. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution (a) Preprocessor: it could not find the file named in an `#include` (a typo). (b) Compiler: the name `std::cout` is used but not declared — `` was not included. (c) Linker: `circle_area` was declared but no object file defines it (e.g. `geometry.cpp` was not compiled or not linked). (d) Linker: two object files define the same non-`inline` variable, typically because the definition `double pi = …;` was put in a header included by two sources (one-definition rule). Fix: declare it `inline constexpr` in the header, or define it in one source file. ::: ::: {#exr-cpp1-rebuild} A project has sources `a.hpp`, `a.cpp`, `b.hpp`, `b.cpp`, `main.cpp`, where `a.cpp` includes `a.hpp`; `b.cpp` includes `b.hpp` and `a.hpp`; `main.cpp` includes `b.hpp`. Each `.cpp` is compiled to a `.o` and the three objects are linked into `app`. Draw the build graph. Which targets are rebuilt when (a) `a.hpp` changes; (b) `b.cpp` changes; (c) `main.cpp` changes? ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution Edges: `a.hpp → a.o`, `a.cpp → a.o`, `b.hpp → b.o`, `a.hpp → b.o`, `b.cpp → b.o`, `b.hpp → main.o`, `main.cpp → main.o`, and `a.o`, `b.o`, `main.o → app`. By @prp-rebuild-set: (a) `a.o`, `b.o`, `app`; (b) `b.o`, `app`; (c) `main.o`, `app`. Note that in (a) `main.o` is *not* rebuilt, even though `main.cpp` uses `b.hpp`, because `main.cpp` does not (transitively) include `a.hpp`. ::: ::: {#exr-cpp1-flags} Compile the `warnings.cpp` program of @sec-flags with `-Werror` added. What happens, and why is `-Werror` a good default for your own projects but a bad idea in code you distribute to others? ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution Compilation fails: each warning becomes an error, so no executable is produced until the three problems are fixed. In your own project this forces warnings to be dealt with immediately. In distributed source code, however, a newer compiler version may introduce *new* warnings, so users would be unable to build perfectly correct code with their compiler; enable `-Werror` in your development and CI builds, not in the default build. ::: ::: {#exr-cpp1-headers} How many lines does the preprocessed translation unit of a file containing only `#include ` and `#include ` have with your compiler? Estimate how many lines the compiler must parse in a project of 200 source files that each include ``, `` and ``. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution Measure with `g++ -std=c++20 -E file.cpp | wc -l`. With GCC 13 and libstdc++ each of these headers expands to tens of thousands of lines, and together (their contents overlap) to a few tens of thousands. With $L$ lines per translation unit and $n = 200$ files, the compiler parses about $nL$ lines — several million — although the headers are identical every time: the redundancy that precompiled headers and C++20 modules remove. ::: ## Further reading {.unnumbered} - @vscodecpp — the official VS Code tutorials: *GCC on Windows via MinGW*, *Microsoft C++ on Windows*, *GCC on Linux*; and the pages on debugging and `c_cpp_properties.json`. - @gccmanual — chapter *GCC Command Options*, in particular *Options to Request or Suppress Warnings*, *Options for Debugging* and *Program Instrumentation Options* (sanitizers). - @bryant2016 — ch. 1 (a tour of the toolchain) and ch. 7 (linking: symbols, relocation, static and shared libraries). - @levine1999 — the classic book on linkers and loaders. - @feldman1979 — the original paper on Make, short and readable. - @serebryany2012 — how AddressSanitizer works (shadow memory), and its cost. - @kernighan1999, ch. 5 — debugging strategies that do not depend on the tool.
